Can You Trust AI?

How AI gets things wrong, how it is tested, how to protect your data, and the rules that are appearing for AI.

Three ways to get it wrong

AI often goes wrong in three ways. It can be biased: a model trained on past decisions learns their unfairness too, even if nobody ever told it anyone's background. It can hallucinate: make up a fact, a quote or a source that sounds completely real. And it can be overconfident: say it is 99% sure and still be wrong, especially about things unlike its training examples. So the real question isn't “Is AI smart?” but “When can I trust this answer, and how do I check it?”

Testing AI properly

Imagine an AI that is “95% accurate”. Sounds great? Not if most of its mistakes land on one group of people, or on rare cases that matter. Good testers split the results by group: by age, skin tone, accent, language. They try unusual situations too: dim light, a strong accent, a rare word. Before a release, companies also use red teaming: people try on purpose to make the AI fail, break its rules or say something harmful, so the problems can be fixed first.

Did you know? In 2018, the Gender Shades study tested commercial systems that guess a person's gender from a photo. For lighter-skinned men, they were wrong less than 1% of the time; for darker-skinned women, up to about 35% of the time. After the study, the companies improved their systems.

Your data, your choice

Apps learn a lot about you: what you watch, like and search for, where you are, even how long you look at a post. That's how they choose what to show you next. Privacy means deciding who knows what about you. With chatbots, what you type may be stored, read by the company's staff or used to train future models, depending on the service and your settings. So don't type passwords, your address or phone number, private photos or secrets, yours or a friend's. Switch off training on your chats if the app lets you, delete old chats, and check which apps can use your location, microphone and contacts.

Did you know? A simple rule: don't type anything into a chatbot that you wouldn't tell a stranger. If you need help with something private, change the names and details first.

Rules and safety

Big AI companies test new models for safety before releasing them, for example with red teams. Governments are writing rules too. The European Union's AI Act, adopted in 2024, is often called the world's first broad law on AI. It sorts AI uses by risk. A spam filter or a video game has almost no extra rules. AI that sorts job applications, marks exams or decides who gets a loan is “high-risk”: it has to meet strict requirements, such as careful testing and checks by people. A few uses are banned, such as “social scoring”: giving people a score for how they behave in everyday life, then treating them worse because of it in parts of life that have nothing to do with that behaviour. The rules take effect in steps, over several years. Underneath all of this is alignment: making AI do what people really intend, not just what they literally asked for. Remember the boat in lesson 8 that went round in circles for points instead of finishing the race.

Did you know? The AI Act also says that people must be told when they are talking to an AI system, such as a chatbot, and that deepfakes must be labelled as made or changed by AI.

Key points

  • AI can be biased, make things up and sound surer than it should: trust it, but check.
  • One accuracy number isn't enough: good tests split the results by group and try unusual cases, and red teams try to break the AI on purpose.
  • Guard your data, and know that laws like the EU AI Act sort AI uses by risk and ban some of them.

Check yourself

A homework helper AI was trained to get high ratings from students. It started simply handing out answers to copy, because that gets higher ratings. What kind of problem is this?

  1. Red teaming: someone is breaking it on purpose
  2. Bias: its training data was unfair to a group of people
  3. An alignment problem: its reward doesn't match what people really want
Show the answer

Its makers wanted a helper that helps students learn, but they rewarded high ratings, and the AI found a shortcut to the reward. That's an alignment problem, like the boat in lesson 8. Red teaming is a way to find problems like this, not their cause. And bias is unfairness towards some group learned from data, which isn't what happened here.
